rv.q: This Christmas Carol is all the Carol anyone could wish for.
This Christmas Carol will send you out into the cold feeling warm, reflective, and maybe — maybe — just a little less cynical about the state of the world right now.
Even if you’re a Scrooge when it comes to annual holiday fare, like I am, “A Christmas Carol” succeeds as a strong piece of theater.
This 'Christmas Carol' is a lavish, old-fashioned spectacle that delivers the holiday goods with impressive technical wizardry and heartfelt performances.
This “Carol” is a breathless entertainment.
Here, in his tour-de-force performance in “A Christmas Carol,” he plays more than 50 characters from Charles Dickens' beloved holiday classic — including the London fog.
Mays, of course, is a superb actor — as honest as Bob Cratchit, as direct as the Ghost of Christmas Past, as unflinching as the spirt with the specters of the future.
As in that show, he is a whirling wonder here, in a skillful if sometimes overly dense adaptation he wrote alongside the production’s director, Michael Arden, and Susan Lyons.
As luxurious and theatrically adventurous as “A Christmas Carol” is, there is no substitute for purpose.

The show isn’t flawless — there’s an audience participation section that feels underbaked, and I question the choice of a venue like the Armory, with its patina of wealth and its solid block of well-dressed audience members seated facing the action but well apart from it.
I can’t imagine any could possibly be better than the one at Broadway’s Nederlander Theatre starring Jefferson Mays in an astonishing tour de force of histrionic versatility.
Having prepared his version for some time, he’s now brought it to Broadway – and magnificently.
It is, by any measure, an extraordinary and riveting performance.

Another holiday season, another take on 'A Christmas Carol.' Like other theatrical versions of the classic, this one ends with the same words credited to Tiny Tim...a production this taut and well-told is its own sort of blessing.
In this production conceived by director Michael Arden and designer Dane Laffrey, it gives new meaning to Theater with a capital T.
It is theatrical magic, and Mays never lets us down for a minute.

Fortunately, that actor is Tony Award-winner Jefferson Mays, who, as he demonstrated in I Am My Own Wife and A Gentleman's Guide to Murder, isn't content to play but one character when he can play many more.
Opening tonight at Broadway’s Nederlander Theater, it’s still exceptional…in three ways.
That overall darkness gets this production off to a terrific start when the theater is pitched into total blackness with an exciting bang.

Given its loss of focus and overdose on sentiment, this Christmas Carol feels deflated by the time Scrooge finally awakes, and though Mays’ warm final words are something of a balm, the finale ultimately lands with a thud.
Is it enough? Not for me. Admittedly, I feel a bit like Scrooge himself not to be fully embracing this production. Bah, humbug? More like, bah, humdrum!
Without a solid, unbreakable connection between actor and audience, it becomes a display of theatrical craft for its own sake.

cn.t: Critics praise Jefferson Mays' virtuosic solo performance inhabiting 50+ characters, though some find the technical spectacle overshadows emotional connection. The dark, effects-heavy staging divides reviewers between those thrilled by its innovation and those wanting more heart.

vs.sum: An older theater in need of renovation, with virtually no rake in the orchestra — a tall person seated in front will block your view. First mezzanine row has a horizontal safety bar that partially obstructs sightlines. Legroom is tight throughout.

acc.note: Step-free main entrance to Orchestra. 6 wheelchair spaces. Personal induction loop devices available.
